## Overview

The Logba people live in the Volta Region of Ghana, east of the Volta Lake in the mountains of the Ghana–Togo borderland. Most Logba settlements lie along the trunk road from Accra to Hohoe. They include Wuinta, Akusame, Adiveme, Andokɔfe, Adzakoe, Alakpeti, Klikpo, and Tota. Tota is situated high in the Ghana–Togo Mountains, while Alakpeti is the commercial centre and Klikpo is traditionally the seat of the head of the Logba people. The Logba are primarily subsistence farmers, producing cassava, maize, yams, and forest fruits, with cocoa, coffee, and sawn mahogany logs as cash crops. Logba is a Kwa language spoken by approximately 7,500 people. The area is known for waterfalls, cliffs, limestone formations, and small caves with minor speleothems.

## Material culture

### Architecture

The sources do identify a family kitchen, a school, and a village through image titles, but provide no descriptive architectural information about them.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The language source gives *zenklǎ* as the Logba word for “pot stand,” describing it as a loanword from Ewe.

## Music & performance

The language source describes Logba as a tonal language with High and Low tones, which can combine on one syllable to produce Rising or Falling contour tones. It also records a few words with rising tone, including *zenklǎ* (“pot stand”) and *tǒ* (“to fell palm trees”), the latter described as ideophonic because it imitates the sound of a palm tree falling. These linguistic examples do not constitute documentation of Logba music or performance traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

No UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription concerns the Logba people in the supplied material.

## Foodways

The sources identify cassava, maize, yams, and forest fruits as products of Logba subsistence farming. They also name cocoa, coffee, and sawn mahogany logs as cash crops. The language source gives *n-dà* as an example meaning “liquor,”.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources do record two accounts concerning Logba origins: one hypothesis proposes that the Logba are descendants of the *makɔ́* people, who fled south after a defeat in the second half of the 18th century, while the Logba people themselves relate that they came together with the Gbe peoples from Ketu. The latter view is also advanced by Dorvlo (2004).

## Language & religion

Logba, which the Logba people call *Ikpana*, is a Kwa language of the Niger–Congo family. The name *Ikpana* means “defenders of truth.” Logba is also referred to as a Ghana–Togo Mountain language; earlier classifications placed it among the Togo Restsprachen, or Togo Remnant languages, and later terminology called the group Central Togo languages. Logba is different from Lukpa of Togo and Benin, which is also sometimes called Logba. The dominant regional language is Ewe, followed by Twi. Most Logba people are bilingual in Ewe; the Logba people article also states that most are bilingual in Ewe and French. The language has nine vowels with ATR vowel harmony, two level tones, and open syllables.
